mockText: 50 items in 100 minutes, with 4 hands-on items (terminal, logs, ordering, diagram), flags and a review screen. Microsoft says 40 to 60 questions in 100 minutes, and some exams add case studies or labs, so this is a stand-in in the middle of that range.
lead: Microsoft's hands-on Azure cert. It proves you can run an Azure environment day to day: users and access, governance, storage, virtual machines and apps, networking, monitoring and backup. It's a common requirement in Azure job posts, and the base for Microsoft's security and architect certs.
objSub: Five skill areas and 15 objectives from Microsoft's AZ-104 study guide (skills measured as of April 17, 2026). Tick them off as you study; progress saves on this device.

cur.label: Apr 2026
cur.note: Same five areas and weights as before; the April 2026 update made small wording changes inside storage, compute, networking and monitoring. No retirement announced. Check the study guide's date before you book.
cur.onote: Official Microsoft skill areas and objectives, in plain words. Microsoft gives weight ranges (20–25%, 15–20%, 20–25%, 15–20%, 10–15%); the bars use the middle of each range.

domains.name: Manage Azure identities and governance
obj: Manage Microsoft Entra users and groups
Create users and groups, manage their properties and licenses, invite external (guest) users, and set up self-service password reset (SSPR).
Manage access to Azure resources
Built-in roles, assigning roles at the right scope, and reading who has which access.
Manage subscriptions and governance
Azure Policy, resource locks, tags, resource groups and subscriptions, budgets and cost alerts, Advisor recommendations, and management groups.

domains.name: Implement and manage storage
obj: Configure access to storage
Storage firewalls and virtual networks, shared access signature (SAS) tokens, stored access policies, access keys, and identity-based access for Azure Files.
Configure and manage storage accounts
Create storage accounts; set redundancy, object replication and encryption; move data with Storage Explorer and AzCopy.
Configure Azure Files and Blob Storage
File shares and blob containers, access tiers, snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files, blob lifecycle rules and versioning.

domains.name: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
obj: Automate deployment with ARM templates or Bicep
Read and change ARM templates and Bicep files, deploy from them, export a deployment, and convert ARM to Bicep.
Create and configure virtual machines
Create VMs, encrypt disks, move VMs between groups, subscriptions or regions, resize and add disks, use availability zones and sets, and run scale sets.
Provision and manage containers
Azure Container Registry, Azure Container Instances and Azure Container Apps, including sizing and scaling.
Create and configure Azure App Service
App Service plans and scaling, web apps, TLS certificates, custom domain names, backups, networking and deployment slots.

domains.name: Implement and manage virtual networking
obj: Configure and manage virtual networks
Virtual networks and subnets, peering, public IP addresses, user-defined routes, and troubleshooting connectivity.
Configure secure access to virtual networks
Network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups, effective security rules, Azure Bastion, and service and private endpoints.
Configure name resolution and load balancing
Azure DNS, internal and public load balancers, and troubleshooting load balancing.

domains.name: Monitor and maintain Azure resources
obj: Monitor resources in Azure
Metrics and log settings in Azure Monitor, log queries, alert rules and action groups, Insights for VMs, storage and networks, and Network Watcher.
Implement backup and recovery
Recovery Services and Backup vaults, backup policies, backup and restore, Azure Site Recovery failover to another region, and backup reports and alerts.

extras.title: Roles and scope
rows: See everything at that scope; change nothing
Create and change resources; can't grant access
User Access Administrator: grants access, can't manage resources
Manage VMs, but not the network or storage they use

extras.title: Storage access
rows: Full access to everything. Rotate it; don't share it
Set rights and an expiry for one service, container or blob
SAS tokens tied to it can be changed or revoked at once
Best choice: no keys, access by user or managed identity

extras.title: NSG rule checks
rows: Inbound: the subnet's NSG is checked first, then the NIC's NSG. Both must allow it.
Outbound: the NIC's NSG first, then the subnet's.
Inside each NSG, rules run by priority: the lowest number wins and checking stops.
Default rules sit at 65000 and up: allow traffic within the VNet, allow the Azure load balancer, deny all other inbound.
Use effective security rules or IP flow verify in Network Watcher to see the result.

extras.title: Network Watcher tools
rows: Is this packet allowed to or from a VM, and by which rule
Where Azure sends traffic from a VM next
Watch reachability and latency over time, with alerts
Record traffic on a VM to read in Wireshark
Log the traffic flows through a VNet or NSG

method: Use the five skill areas above. Identity and compute are the biggest at 20–25% each.
Do Microsoft Learn's free AZ-104 learning paths, then a full video course or an exam cram to tie it together.
Work through Microsoft's free AZ-104 GitHub labs in a personal Azure account. Delete each resource group when you're done so it doesn't cost money.
Flashcards for roles, storage access options, redundancy, NSG rule order and which backup tool does what.
Microsoft's free practice assessment, then timed practice exams. Rebuild in the portal anything you missed.
tips: Associate exams let you open Microsoft Learn during the test. It's slow, so use it only to confirm a detail, not to learn a topic.
Many questions turn on the scope of a role or policy: management group, subscription, resource group or resource.
Some sections, like case studies, can't be reopened once you finish them. Answer everything in a section before you move on.
If you've never created a peering, an NSG rule or a backup policy in the portal, do it before exam day.

items: The official skills list and change log.
Exam details, free learning paths and scheduling.
Microsoft's step-by-step lab instructions. Run them in your own account.
Use a personal account and card, never a government card or work data. Set a budget alert first.
Try case studies and the other question types before test day.
Pick one full course with labs and finish it.

quiz.q: A tech must be able to start, stop and resize the VMs in the ops-rg resource group, and nothing else. What's the BEST assignment?
o: Virtual Machine Contributor at the ops-rg scope
Right. It covers managing VMs, and the resource group scope keeps it to those VMs.
Contributor at the subscription scope
It works, but it lets the tech change every resource in the subscription.
Owner at the ops-rg scope
Owner can also grant access to others. That's more than the tech needs.
Reader at the ops-rg scope
Reader can see the VMs but can't start, stop or resize them.

quiz.q: Every new resource group must have a CostCenter tag, and creating one without it should fail. What should you use?
o: An Azure Policy with the Deny effect that requires the tag on resource groups
Right. Deny blocks anything that doesn't meet the rule.
A resource lock on the subscription
Locks stop deletes or changes. They don't require tags.
A custom RBAC role
RBAC controls who can act, not what settings a resource must have.
An Azure Policy with the Audit effect
Audit only reports non-compliant resources. They still get created.

quiz.q: Users should be able to reset their own passwords after verifying with the Authenticator app, without calling the help desk. What do you configure?
o: Self-service password reset (SSPR)
Right. SSPR lets users reset their password after proving who they are.
Conditional Access
Conditional Access sets sign-in rules. It doesn't reset passwords.
Privileged Identity Management
PIM gives just-in-time admin roles.
Guest user invitations
Invitations add external users.

quiz.q: An outside app needs read-only access to one blob container for 24 hours. You must not share the account key. What should you give it?
o: A SAS token with read permission and a 24-hour expiry
Right. A shared access signature limits the rights, the target and the time.
The storage account access key
That gives full access to the whole account, with no expiry.
Make the container public
Then anyone on the internet can read it, forever.
Owner role on the storage account
Far too much access for a read-only, temporary need.

quiz.q: Dozens of SAS tokens were issued from a stored access policy, and one leaked. What's the fastest way to make all of them stop working without affecting other apps?
o: Change or delete the stored access policy
Right. Tokens tied to a stored access policy are revoked when the policy changes.
Regenerate the storage account key
It revokes the tokens, but it also breaks every other app that uses that key.
Delete the blobs
That destroys the data, not the tokens.
Make the container private
SAS tokens still work on a private container.

quiz.q: Blobs not changed for 30 days should move to the Cool tier and be deleted after 365 days, automatically. What should you set up?
o: A lifecycle management policy
Right. Lifecycle rules move and delete blobs based on age.
Object replication
That copies blobs to another account.
Soft delete
Soft delete keeps deleted data for a while. It doesn't move data by age.
A nightly AzCopy script
It could work, but it's custom code to maintain when a built-in rule does the job.

quiz.q: Two VMs running the same app must survive a datacenter failure in the region. Which option gives the highest availability?
o: Put them in different availability zones
Right. Zones are separate datacenters; Microsoft's SLA for VMs across two or more zones is 99.99%.
Put them in an availability set
Sets spread VMs across racks in one datacenter. They don't survive losing the datacenter.
Put them in a scale set in one zone
One zone means one datacenter failure takes both.
Use one larger VM
A single VM is a single point of failure.

quiz.q: You must deploy the same virtual network and VMs to dev, test and prod, the same way every time. What should you use?
o: A Bicep file or ARM template with parameters for each environment
Right. Infrastructure as code deploys the same design repeatedly, changing only the parameters.
Build each one by hand in the portal
Slow, and the three will drift apart.
Clone the dev VMs
Cloning VMs doesn't rebuild the network and settings.
Azure Advisor
Advisor makes recommendations. It doesn't deploy anything.

quiz.q: You want to test a new version of a web app in App Service, then move it into production with no downtime. What should you use?
o: Deployment slots, then swap
Right. You deploy to a staging slot, test it, then swap it with production.
Scale out to more instances
That adds capacity. It doesn't stage a new version.
Back up and restore the app
Restoring isn't a release process and causes downtime.
Map a custom domain
Domains change the URL, not the version.

quiz.q: You need to run one container quickly, without managing servers or a Kubernetes cluster. What's the simplest choice?
o: Azure Container Instances
Right. ACI runs a container on demand with nothing else to set up.
Azure Kubernetes Service
AKS runs a whole cluster. That's far more than one container needs.
A VM with Docker installed
Then you're managing a server.
Azure Container Registry
ACR stores images. It doesn't run them.

quiz.q: VNet A is peered with VNet B, and VNet B is peered with VNet C. Can a VM in A reach a VM in C?
o: No. Peering isn't transitive; peer A with C, or route through a hub with a firewall or gateway
Right. Each peering only connects the two networks in it.
Yes. Traffic flows through B automatically
Peering doesn't pass traffic through a middle network.
Yes, but only for DNS traffic
There's no such exception.
Only if all three are in the same region
Region doesn't matter. Peering is never transitive.

quiz.q: A VM can't be reached on port 443. Both its subnet and its network interface have NSGs. What's the fastest way to see what's blocking it?
o: Check the effective security rules, or run IP flow verify in Network Watcher
Right. They combine both NSGs and name the rule that allows or denies the traffic.
Set up Connection Monitor
That watches reachability over time. It's not the quickest way to find a blocking rule.
Check Azure DNS
DNS resolves names. It doesn't block ports.
Delete both NSGs
That removes all your protection. Never fix it that way.

quiz.q: An app in a VNet must reach Azure SQL Database over a private IP address, and public network access to the database must be turned off. What should you use?
o: A private endpoint
Right. It gives the database a private IP inside your VNet.
A service endpoint
Traffic stays on Microsoft's network, but the database still uses its public endpoint.
An NSG rule
An NSG filters traffic. It doesn't give the database a private address.
A VPN Gateway
A VPN connects networks. It doesn't put the database in the VNet.

quiz.q: The on-call team must get an email when a VM's CPU stays above 90% for 10 minutes. What do you create?
o: A metric alert rule with an action group that emails the team
Right. The rule watches the metric; the action group decides who gets told and how.
A diagnostic setting
That sends logs somewhere. It doesn't alert anyone.
An Azure Advisor recommendation
Advisor gives advice, not real-time alerts.
A Log Analytics workspace
A workspace stores logs. You still need an alert rule.

quiz.q: VMs must keep replicating to another region so you can fail over quickly during a regional outage. What should you use?
o: Azure Site Recovery
Right. Site Recovery replicates VMs and handles failover and failback.
Azure Backup
Backup restores data from recovery points. It isn't built for fast regional failover.
Disk snapshots
Snapshots are point-in-time copies, not ongoing replication with failover.
A VM scale set
Scale sets add instances in one region.

pbqs.title: Pick the role and the scope
pbqs.scenario: Five people need Azure access. Pick the least-privilege built-in role and the narrowest scope that still works.

rows.req: An auditor must see everything in the subscription but change nothing.
rows.why: Reader at the subscription lets them see it all without changing anything.

rows.req: A tech starts, stops and resizes VMs in ops-rg only.
rows.why: VM Contributor covers VMs; the resource group scope keeps it there.

rows.req: A team lead manages everything in app-rg and gives teammates access to it.
rows.why: Granting access needs Owner (or User Access Admin). Scope it to app-rg.

rows.req: A developer manages one web app and must not grant access.
rows.why: Contributor can manage but can't grant access; scope it to that one app.

rows.req: A security admin manages role assignments across the subscription, not the resources.
rows.why: User Access Administrator handles access only, at the subscription scope.

pbqs.title: Pick the Network Watcher tool
pbqs.scenario: Six troubleshooting tasks. Pick the tool for each. Each answer is used once; two are distractors.

items.text: Is TCP 443 from 10.1.0.4 to this VM allowed or denied, and by which rule?
items.why: IP flow verify tests one flow and names the rule that decides it.

items.text: Traffic from a VM never reaches the office network. Where does Azure send it next?
items.why: Next hop shows the route Azure picks, like a gateway or a firewall.

items.text: See every NSG rule that applies to a NIC, combined from the subnet and the NIC.
items.why: Effective security rules merge both NSGs into one list.

items.text: Record five minutes of real traffic on a VM to open in Wireshark.
items.why: Packet capture records the traffic itself.

items.text: Keep a record of every allowed and denied flow for later review.
items.why: Flow logs record traffic flows to storage for analysis.

items.text: Watch a website's reachability and latency all week and alert if it drops.
items.why: Connection monitor checks continuously and can alert.

pbqs.title: Pick the storage feature
pbqs.scenario: Six requests came in about the unit's storage accounts. Pick the feature that handles each one. Each is used once; one is a distractor.

rows.req: A vendor needs to upload to one container for 7 days, without the account key.
rows.why: A SAS token sets the rights, the container and the expiry.

rows.req: You want to be able to revoke a whole group of SAS tokens at once.
rows.why: Tokens tied to a stored access policy stop working when you change the policy.

rows.req: Old blobs should move to Cool, then Archive, then be deleted.
rows.why: Lifecycle rules act on blobs by age.

rows.req: Someone deleted a file share last week; get it back.
rows.why: Soft delete keeps deleted shares for a set number of days.

rows.req: Only the unit's VNet and office IP may reach the account.
rows.why: The storage firewall limits access to chosen networks and IPs.

rows.req: Keep an on-premises file server in sync with an Azure file share.
rows.why: Azure File Sync caches and syncs Azure Files on Windows servers.

keep.text: Microsoft role-based certs last one year. Renew for free by passing a short, open-book online assessment on Microsoft Learn.
keep.after: The assessment opens 6 months before your cert expires, and you can retake it as often as you need until then. Passing adds one year.

keep.text: No Azure cert is on the DoD 8140 matrix (V3.0). For a coded billet, you still need one that is, like Security+ or Cloud+.
keep.after: Government Azure work often runs in Azure Government, a separate cloud for U.S. agencies. The admin skills are the same.

keep.text: Check that CG COOL lists the credential before you request funding.
keep.after: Renewals are free, so the exam fee is the only cost.
